title: High-rate qLDPC processors
authors: Aditya Bhardwaj, Muzhou Ma, Nadine Meister, Robbie King, Dolev Bluvstein, John Preskill, Madelyn Cain, Qian Xu, Hsin-Yuan Huang
abstract: Despite significant progress on quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, building qLDPC processors that are high-rate, high-throughput, hardware-friendly, and fast-to-decode remains a challenge. We introduce mitten codes, a family of qLDPC processor codes of encoding rate $20\%$ and check weight $9$, based on non-abelian groups. Their non-abelian structure evades distance bounds constraining abelian counterparts, allowing mitten codes to reach distance $18$ and beyond with just a few hundred data qubits. The logical operators of a mitten code are related by the group action, yielding a modular, low-overhead logical toolkit: full Clifford operations follow from bridging two reusable seed surgery gadgets or from a single fixed extractor. Furthermore, qLDPC processors based on mitten codes support high-rate surgery that executes many logical measurements in parallel, and parallel magic-state injection into all logical qubits at once. Under circuit-level noise, with our fast decoder, the $[\![300,60,14]\!]$ mitten code achieves, without extrapolation, a block logical error rate of ${\sim}10^{-11}$ per round at $0.1\%$ physical error rate (PER), while the $[\![ 975,195,\leq 24 ]\!]$ code reaches ${\sim}10^{-8}$ at $0.4\%$ PER. Decoding $15$ billion surgery experiments on the $[\![540,108,18]\!]$ code at $0.1\%$ PER, we observe only two logical failures, demonstrating a qLDPC processor capable of running ${\sim}10^{10}$ logical operations. Our decoder is compatible with sub-millisecond average latency per logical cycle, sufficient for real-time decoding on neutral atom hardware. Discovered by an end-to-end design pipeline built on sQetch, a distance estimator orders of magnitude faster than existing tools, and mapping efficiently onto near-term neutral atom and superconducting hardware, mitten codes open a practical path toward fault-tolerant quantum computation.
summary: The paper introduces 'mitten codes,' a novel class of qLDPC codes derived from non-abelian groups, to address the major hurdles in building scalable quantum processors. By demonstrating high performance metrics—such as achieving $10^{-11}$ logical error rates with manageable physical qubits—and by developing automated design pipelines for hardware mapping, they propose a practical path toward fault-tolerant quantum computation on near-term platforms.
main_problem: The primary challenge is designing quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) processors that are simultaneously high-rate, high-throughput, hardware-friendly, and fast to decode for fault-tolerant computation.
main_result: The authors introduce 'mitten codes,' a family of qLDPC codes based on non-abelian groups, which overcome distance limitations of abelian codes and demonstrate achieving logical error rates as low as $10^{-11}$ at achievable physical error rates.
method: They developed an end-to-end design pipeline using sQetch to discover these codes, proving their feasibility through rigorous simulation of syndrome extraction and hardware placement optimization (Spectral Placement).
model_or_system: The work focuses on abstract qLDPC processor models implemented via 'mitten codes,' which are lifted product codes over non-abelian groups. The physical realization is mapped onto near-term neutral atom arrays and superconducting qubit architectures.
key_observables: Block logical error rate ($\sim 10^{-11}$), processing capacity, throughput (logical operations per cycle), and hardware complexity metrics like Tiers, Length, and TSVs.
important_parameters: Encoding rate of $20\%$, check weight of 9, physical error rate (PER) up to $0.4\%$, and sub-millisecond decoding latency.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the non-abelian structure is key to bypassing distance bounds; hardware feasibility relies on mapping complex graph structures onto discrete superconducting or neutral atom lattices.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the code structure, the three-level discovery pipeline (sQetch), and detailed comparisons of hardware complexities (Tiers, Length) for various codes using placement algorithms.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the general challenge to introducing mitten codes as a solution. It details the theoretical advantages of non-abelian groups, presents performance benchmarks (error rates/throughput), and concludes with detailed analyses on hardware mapping complexity (thickness and physical layout optimization).
why_interesting: This work provides concrete, quantifiable metrics for assessing fault tolerance beyond simple error correction thresholds by integrating code theory with practical constraints like circuit depth and physical routing overhead.
